**Title:** Halcyon Threshold: Identifying and Supporting Neglected High-Impact Work in AI Governance & Safety

**Problem:** Superintelligent AI arrival may be humanity's most important inflection point, yet talent and resources are concentrated in a few institutions (major labs, well-funded orgs). Promising independent work in evals, governance analysis, safety research, and community coordination goes unfunded and under-resourced.

**Approach:** Halcyon Threshold will operate as an identifying and enabling mechanism for neglected, high-impact opportunities in AI governance and safety through:

1. **Targeted grants and stipends** ($500–$5k per project) to researchers, analysts, and organizers working on specific neglected problems

- Track outcomes from Phase 2 grantees

- Consider raising additional funding or organizing as formal fund

## Success Metrics

**Year 1 targets:**
- 10-15 grants distributed
- 30%+ of projects lead to tangible outcomes (publications, policy briefs, community impact)
- Documented insights into what makes high-impact AI safety work possible
- Foundation for multi-year funding program

**Longer-term vision:**
- Establish Halcyon Threshold as known source for underfunded high-impact work
- Grow from $25k → $100k+ annual funding
- Possibly transition to formal entity (nonprofit, fiscal sponsorship) by Year 2-3

---

## Why This Matters

The arrival of superintelligent AI is not evenly distributed in probability space. Small decisions made by a few people in the next 1-5 years likely matter enormously. Most superintelligence-relevant work happens inside labs, policy orgs, or well-funded institutes. 

But there are talented people outside these structures doing important work on evals, governance, safety analysis, and community coordination who are resource-constrained.

Halcyon Threshold's role: **Find these people. Give them resources to do better work. Learn what works. Scale it.**

This is high-leverage use of a thoughtful person + a modest amount of capital.

---

## Contingency: If Grant Doesn't Materialize

With just Morgan's $2k + volunteer time:
- Fund 1-2 small grants ($800-1200 each) to test the model
- Document what you learn
- Use that for larger fundraising next year
- Pivot to community-building focus (lower-cost, meaningful output)

The core insight holds: funding others' work is higher-leverage than doing work directly.

Halcyon Threshold

Identifying and supporting neglected high-impact work in AI safety and governance

Who We Are

Halcyon Threshold is a research and funding initiative dedicated to ensuring the best possible outcome for superintelligent AI arrival.

We believe the most important inflection point in human history may happen in this decade. We also believe that good outcomes are far from guaranteed—they require thoughtful work by talented people, much of it outside mainstream institutions.

The Problem

Most superintelligence-relevant work happens inside a few labs and well-funded organizations. But there is important, underfunded work happening elsewhere: independent research on AI evaluation and interpretability, governance analysis, community coordination, safety policy analysis, and more.

These projects often lack resources that would unlock significant impact.

What We Do

1. Identify High-Impact Opportunities

We seek out promising projects and researchers working on neglected problems in AI safety, governance, and related fields—the work that deserves resources but often doesn't have them.

2. Provide Direct Support

We offer grants and stipends ($1,500–$5,000 typical range) to fund specific projects, research, analysis, or organizational work that advances AI safety outcomes.

3. Build Community & Learning

We connect researchers and practitioners, and we document what we learn about what actually works in making AI safety progress possible.

We're Looking For

We invite applications from people working on:

  • AI evaluation & interpretability — Novel approaches to understanding or testing frontier AI systems
  • Governance analysis — Research on policy, regulation, or institutional design for AI safety
  • Safety & robustness research — Technical or conceptual work on AI alignment, safety, or robustness
  • Community building — Organizing, connecting researchers, or creating infrastructure for the field
  • Other neglected high-impact work — If you're doing something important in AI safety that isn't well-funded, we want to hear from you

Ideal candidates: Individual researchers, small teams, or organizations with concrete plans, clear metrics, and (often) constraints on funding or institutional support.

How to Apply

We accept applications on a rolling basis. To apply:

  1. Email us at grants@halcyonthreshold.org with:
    • Brief description of your project (what, why it matters, why you)
    • Specific goals and timeline (3–12 months)
    • How much funding you need and why
    • Your background/experience
  2. We'll review and follow up within 2 weeks
  3. We aim to fund promising projects within 4 weeks of acceptance

Applications are currently closed but will reopen in early December 2026. Sign up below to be notified.

Our Approach

  • Independence. We're not beholden to any lab, policy body, or funding source beyond our own commitments. We evaluate work on its merits.
  • Contrarianism welcome. If you're working on something others think is wrong or unimportant, that's often a sign you're exploring territory that matters.
  • Speed. We want decisions fast so you can get funded quickly.
  • Learning. We'll track what happens with our grantees and publish what we learn—both to improve our own process and to help the field.

Contact

Halcyon Threshold
Email: grants@halcyonthreshold.org
Organization: Morgan Hale, Founder

Halcyon Threshold is an independent research and funding initiative focused on advancing AI safety and governance. We are not affiliated with any laboratory, corporation, or policy body.

© 2026 Halcyon Threshold. All rights reserved.

# Halcyon Threshold Grants Program — Application Framework

## Purpose

This framework guides the design and evaluation of grant applications. It's meant to be:
- **Simple**: Applicants can write strong proposals in 2-4 hours
- **Flexible**: Different types of work (research, evals, policy, organizing) all fit
- **Rigorous**: We can fairly compare different approaches
- **Fast**: We can make decisions quickly

---

## Application Form (Target: 1-2 pages)

Applicants should provide:

### 1. Project Summary
**Question:** What are you working on? (2-3 sentences)

**What we're looking for:** Clear, honest description. Technical jargon is fine; opacity is not.

**Example strong answer:** 
> I'm building a dataset and methodology for evaluating whether large language models maintain consistent values across different prompting strategies. This is important because value drift under adversarial prompting is a potential failure mode we don't have good measurements for. My hypothesis is that current evaluations miss subtle but important failures.

### 2. Why This Matters
**Question:** Why does this problem matter for AI safety/governance? Why now?

**What we're looking for:**
- Honest assessment of importance
- Why this is neglected (what's missing? why haven't others funded it?)
- Clear theory of change (how does your work improve outcomes?)
- Avoid: vague claims of importance, overstating impact

**Example strong answer:**
> Frontier model developers prioritize benchmarks that show improvement over time. Public-facing evaluations are therefore biased toward the lab's interests. Independent evaluation methodology would give policymakers and oversight bodies tools to assess frontier systems without relying on lab-provided data. This is neglected because it's unglamorous and requires domain expertise in both ML and policy. But it directly enables the governance infrastructure we'll need.

### 3. Your Qualifications
**Question:** What makes you the right person for this?

**What we're looking for:**
- Relevant experience/background
- Specific skills that matter for this project
- Track record (if available)
- Intellectual honesty about gaps
- We fund people early in careers too—honesty > credentials

**Example strong answer:**
> I have 4 years of industry ML experience and have published on interpretability. I'm not a policy expert, but I've spent the last 6 months embedded with a policy research org learning how evaluation is actually used in practice. This hybrid background is unusual and I think it's exactly what's needed for this work.

### 4. Specific Plan & Deliverables
**Question:** What will you actually produce? How will you measure success?

**What we're looking for:**
- Concrete outputs (papers, datasets, code, analysis, reports, events, etc.)
- Specific milestones (what by when?)
- Clear success criteria (how do we know if this worked?)
- Realistic timeline
- Avoid: vague aspirations, moving targets

**Example strong answer:**
> By March 31, I'll have:
> 1. Developed a standardized evaluation protocol (document, 10-20 pages) tested on 3 existing models
> 2. Created a public dataset of 500 test cases + human evaluator labels
> 3. Detailed write-up of findings regarding value consistency failures
> 
> Success = protocol is used by at least 2 independent research groups by Q2 2027.

### 5. Budget & Timeline
**Question:** How much funding do you need and why? What's your timeline?

**What we're looking for:**
- Honest breakdown (salary, materials, operations, etc.)
- Why this amount? (what does it unlock?)
- Timeline: 3-12 months typical
- Breakdown of time allocation
- Avoid: inflated numbers, vague budgets

**Example strong answer:**
> $4,000 over 4 months:
> - $2,500 for 200 hours of my time at reduced rate (working ~12 hrs/week on this)
> - $800 for AWS compute for model evaluation
> - $500 for human evaluator payments (50 hours at $10/hr)
> - $200 miscellaneous (literature access, tools)
> 
> Without funding, I can only work ~3 hrs/week (vs 12), extending timeline to 12+ months and losing momentum.

### 6. What Happens After?
**Question:** If this is successful, what's the next phase?

**What we're looking for:**
- Realistic assessment of impact and limitations
- Plans for scaling/extending if promising
- How others could build on this
- Honesty about uncertainty
- Connection to broader goals

**Example strong answer:**
> If successful, this evaluation protocol could be adopted by independent evaluators or policy researchers. I'm not building a company; the goal is to create a reusable tool. Next steps would be: (1) refine based on initial feedback, (2) publish detailed methodology paper, (3) explore partnerships with policy organizations for deployment. I'd likely seek follow-on funding to scale testing to more models and more evaluators.

---

## Evaluation Rubric

**Scoring: 1–5 scale per category**

### 1. Problem Importance (25% weight)
- **5:** Addresses critical gap in AI safety/governance; immediate relevance
- **4:** Addresses important gap; relevant to multiple stakeholders
- **3:** Addresses real but more peripheral problem
- **2:** Problem is real but solution path unclear
- **1:** Importance not clearly established

*Notes:* We're looking for work that matters for actual AI outcomes, not just academic interest. Neglected problems get bonus points.

### 2. Neglectedness (20% weight)
- **5:** Almost no one else is working on this; clear gap
- **4:** Very few people/orgs addressing it; obvious underfunding
- **3:** Some work exists but underfunded relative to importance
- **2:** Moderately crowded field but with gaps
- **1:** Well-funded, competitive space

*Notes:* Our value-add is funding work others won't. If it's already well-funded, we should be skeptical.

### 3. Quality of Plan (25% weight)
- **5:** Concrete, realistic, well-thought-out; clear success metrics
- **4:** Good plan; minor gaps or unrealistic timeline
- **3:** Decent plan but some ambiguity; could be more specific
- **2:** Vague plan; unclear success criteria or approach
- **1:** Plan is unclear or unrealistic

*Notes:* We want ambitious but achievable. Plans that change based on reality are good. Unrealistic confidence is bad.

### 4. Applicant Capability (20% weight)
- **5:** Highly relevant background; proven track record; intellectual honesty
- **4:** Strong relevant background; good track record
- **3:** Some relevant experience; no obvious red flags
- **2:** Limited background; would need significant support
- **1:** Significant gaps; unclear why they're the right person

*Notes:* Track record matters but isn't everything. Early-career people with insight and honesty score well. Overconfidence scores poorly.

### 5. Value for Money (10% weight)
- **5:** $X funding unlocks disproportionate value (e.g., removing key bottleneck)
- **4:** Efficient use of capital; good ROI
- **3:** Reasonable budget for the work
- **2:** Budget seems high relative to outputs
- **1:** Poor value proposition

*Notes:* Cheaper isn't always better. A $5k grant that frees someone for a quarter to focus is better value than $500 for a side project.

---

## Decision Framework

**Approve if:**
- Average score ≥ 4.0, AND
- No serious red flags (e.g., applicant misrepresenting credentials), AND
- Budget is reasonable, AND
- We believe the work will actually happen

**Approve with conditions if:**
- Score is 3.5–3.9, AND
- We can address concerns with a conversation

**Waitlist if:**
- Score is 3.0–3.4, AND
- We can fund them if budget allows after first round

**Decline if:**
- Score < 3.0, OR
- Serious red flags, OR
- Work is better suited to other funders

---

## Target Applicant Profiles

**We're especially interested in:**

1. **Independent researchers** with a specific evaluation or analysis project
2. **Small teams** (2-4 people) doing underfunded safety research
3. **Early-career people** with good ideas but limited institutional support
4. **Policy/governance researchers** working on AI-specific questions
5. **Researchers leaving labs** who want to continue work independently
6. **People with specific technical skills** (interpretability, evals, etc.) who want to apply them to neglected problems
7. **Community builders** organizing or connecting researchers
8. **Methodologists** developing better approaches to evaluation/research

**Less ideal (but not disqualified):**
- Established researchers at well-funded institutions (unless working on specific underfunded project)
- Broad organizational work without concrete deliverables
- Academic dissertations (though sometimes)
- Pure community-building without research outputs

---

## Rough Timeline

**December 2026:** Open applications, target 30-50 submissions
**January 2027:** Evaluate, make decisions, fund first wave (8-12 grants)
**Feb-March 2027:** Distribute funds, support grantees, begin tracking outcomes
**April 2027:** Synthesis and learning

---

## Reporting & Outcomes Tracking

We ask all grantees to report:
- **Month 2:** Progress update (500 words)
- **Final:** Completion report (1,000-2,000 words) with:
  - What you actually produced
  - What surprised you
  - What you learned about the problem
  - How the work could be used/extended
  - Whether this funding enabled work that wouldn't have happened otherwise

This helps us understand what worked and what we should fund differently next round.

# Halcyon Threshold Grants — Target Opportunities & Potential Applicants

## Neglected Problem Areas (Ranked by Impact + Neglectedness)

### 1. Independent Frontier Model Evaluation
**Why neglected:** Lab-developed evaluations are biased toward showing progress. Policy-makers and safety researchers lack truly independent evaluations.

**What's missing:**
- Methodologies for evaluating frontier models without lab cooperation
- Datasets/benchmarks for red-teaming or adversarial testing
- Clear frameworks for technical evaluation that policy bodies can understand
- Reproducible results across different eval frameworks

**Potential grantees:** Sam Whitlock (indie evals person), technical researchers interested in methodology

---

### 2. AI Governance Infrastructure
**Why neglected:** Most governance work happens inside policy institutions or labs. Independent research on what governance actually needs to work is underfunded.

**What's missing:**
- Technical research for policymakers (how to actually implement frontier model licensing?)
- International coordination frameworks (how do different countries' policies interact?)
- Enforcement mechanism research (what does verification actually look like?)
- Case studies from existing governance efforts

**Potential grantees:** Governance researchers (Tomasz Wrona at Corvid?), policy analysts interested in AI

---

### 3. Interpretability & Mechanistic Understanding
**Why neglected:** Big labs are doing this internally. Independent interpretability research often lacks compute resources or institutional support.

**What's missing:**
- Open-source interpretability tools and methodologies
- Research on whether current interpretability methods scale to frontier models
- Systematic studies of specific failure modes
- Reproducible interpretability work

**Potential grantees:** Lena Fischbach (interpretability researcher), researchers leaving labs, academics interested in scaling interpretability

---

### 4. Safety Research Methodology
**Why neglected:** How do we actually measure safety properties? This is foundational but not flashy.

**What's missing:**
- Datasets for safety benchmarking
- Formal frameworks for defining "safe behavior"
- Reproducible measurement protocols
- Comparative analysis of different safety approaches

**Potential grantees:** Technical researchers, academics in ML safety, people with methodology background

---

### 5. Community Coordination & Knowledge Infrastructure
**Why neglected:** Most researchers are siloed. There's no systematic way to share findings, coordinate on problems, or track progress.

**What's missing:**
- Shared datasets and benchmarks (beyond what labs publish)
- Forum/infrastructure for independent researchers to coordinate
- Regular synthesis of research findings
- Bridges between technical researchers, policy, and governance

**Potential grantees:** Asha Venkataraman (forum moderator), people interested in organizing

### Good fit but lower priority:

   - Noted as "busy" but interpretability is key gap
   - Might have specific project underfunded by institutional constraints
   
5. **Tomasz Wrona** (twrona@corvidinstitute.org) — Governance

**Opportunity:** Fund high-quality researchers in underrepresented regions (Canada, Australia, Asia, etc.)

**Potential impact:** Medium-high (new perspectives, geographic distribution of capability)

### C. Underfunded Technical Areas
Some highly important technical areas have very few researchers:

- **AI warfare/security implications** (how does AI change military dynamics?)
- **Economics of AI scaling** (at what point do scaling laws break? What's the actual cost frontier?)
- **Reproducibility of frontier results** (can we replicate claimed capabilities?)
- **Benchmark saturation** (when do benchmarks stop being useful?)

**Opportunity:** Fund specialists in these areas to do focused research

**Potential impact:** High (uncovering important unknowns)

Most valuable insights come from bridging technical and policy, or bridging different sub-fields.

# HR Conversation — Talking Points for Morgan

**Context:** Dorrance Logistics has an outside activities disclosure requirement. Morgan needs to clear voluntary work with Halcyon Threshold before making public statements.

---

## Opening Position

"I've started working on something outside Dorrance that I wanted to clear with you. It's volunteer work on AI governance and safety policy, separate from my role here. I'm doing it through an organization called Halcyon Threshold and wanted to make sure there are no conflicts."

---

## Key Points to Make

### 1. It's Genuinely Separate
- **Timing:** Evenings and weekends only
- **No resources:** Using personal time and personal money, no Dorrance resources
- **Different field:** AI governance; separate from logistics/supply chain
- **No direct conflicts:** Not competing with Dorrance, not representing Dorrance

### 2. It's Appropriate to Disclose
- "I think transparency is better. I'd rather disclose now than have questions later."
- Show you take the disclosure requirements seriously
- Frame as: "I'm following the spirit of the policy, not trying to hide anything"

### 3. There Are No Conflicts of Interest
- You're not making policy statements attacking Dorrance
- You're not using Dorrance information or relationships
- You're not taking opportunities that rightfully belong to Dorrance
- The work is on AI governance, not supply chain/logistics

### 4. This Actually Makes You Better at Dorrance
- More informed on emerging tech issues
- Better understanding of policy landscape
- More engaged and motivated
- (Optional: "It keeps me intellectually stimulated in an area I care about")

---

## How to Frame the Work

**Do say:**
- "Research and funding for high-potential work in AI safety"
- "Identifying promising researchers and projects underfunded in the field"
- "Independent evaluation and community coordination"
- "Small-scale grants program"

**Don't overstate:**
- Avoid: "I'm building a company" (they might worry about IP or attention)
- Avoid: "I'm making policy" (they might worry about public statements)
- Avoid: "This could be huge" (they might worry about commitment)
- Avoid: "I'm speaking as a representative of AI safety movement" (they might worry about liability)

---

## Likely HR Questions

### Q: "How much time will this take?"
**Answer:** "Evenings and weekends, estimate 5-10 hours per week. Won't impact my Dorrance work."

### Q: "Will you be making public statements in your personal name?"
**Answer:** "Yes, in my personal capacity as the founder of Halcyon Threshold. Nothing that claims to represent Dorrance or makes statements on behalf of Dorrance."

### Q: "Could there be conflicts?"
**Answer:** "I don't see any. We're focused on AI safety governance research, not competing with Dorrance. I'm not using Dorrance information or relationships. I'm not making positions that conflict with Dorrance's interests. If anything comes up, I'll bring it to you first."

### Q: "Does this need formal approval or can you just disclose it?"
**Answer:** "I want to follow whatever process makes sense. Happy to do whatever paperwork you need. This is just voluntary outside work."

### Q: "What if this grows or becomes a company?"
**Answer:** "Right now it's just volunteer research and small grants. If that changes, I'll loop back in with you. But the plan is staying volunteer-based and modest in scale."

---

## If They Ask for Paperwork

**What to expect:**
- They may ask you to fill out the annual outside activities disclosure form
- They may ask for clarification on time commitment and scope
- They may want to see the organization's materials (website, mission statement)

**Have ready:**
- STRATEGY.md or mission statement
- Time estimate (5-10 hrs/week)
- Any formal organization docs (if you've created them)
- Website link when it's live

---

## If They Say "No"

**This would be surprising, but possible responses:**
1. "Can I do it under a pseudonym or completely anonymously?" (harder to manage)
2. "Can we revisit this in 6 months?" (might work)
3. "What if I reduce to evenings-only?" (compromise)
4. "Would X type of work be acceptable instead?" (negotiate scope)

**Fallback:** Even if your personal name isn't approved for public statements, Halcyon Threshold can still operate independently (organization-level rather than person-level).

---

## If They Say "Yes"

**Great! Then:**
- Get any required paperwork/disclosure in writing
- Clarify: "So I can make public statements as long as they're in my personal capacity, not representing Dorrance?"
- Follow up with: "I'll keep you in the loop if scope changes"
- Thank them and move forward

---

## Tone

**Overall approach:** Professional, transparent, collaborative
- Not defensive
- Not seeking permission to do something controversial (it's not)
- Not minimizing the work (show you take it seriously)
- Not maximizing it either (don't oversell impact)

**Goal:** Leave them thinking "this is fine, they're being transparent and responsible"

---

## After the Conversation

**Regardless of outcome:**
- Send follow-up email confirming what you discussed and what they approved
- Document any limitations they placed
- Flag the date this was cleared (useful if anyone questions it later)
- Include in your annual outside activities disclosure (if required)

# AI Safety Funding Landscape Analysis (Nov 2026)

## Current Funding Ecosystem

### Major Institutional Funding
- **Open Philanthropy** (~$100M+ committed to AI risk)
- **Survival and Flourishing Fund** 
- **Center for AI Safety** (funding through partnerships)
- **Lab-internal funding** (OpenAI, DeepMind, Anthropic internal budgets)
- **Academic funding** (NSF, DOE, international)

**Characteristics:**
- Large ($50k-$500k+ grants typical)
- Institutional or credentialed applicants
- Complex application processes
- Multi-year funding

### Emerging Smaller Grants
1. **Emberfall Fund** — $5-25k rapid grants (closes Nov 30)
   - Relatively new entrant
   - Fast decisions (2 weeks target)
   - Less formal than traditional foundations
   - Target: under-resourced promising work

2. **Compute Commons** — Up to $3k cloud credits
   - Specific: only computing resources
   - Rolling applications
   - For independent researchers
   - Fills specific bottleneck (compute access)

3. **Alignment Commons** — Forum + post publication
   - Infrastructure, not direct funding
   - Amplifies work, creates visibility

### The Gap Halcyon Threshold Fills

**Funding types that exist:**
- ✅ Very large grants ($100k+) for institutions
- ✅ Computing resources (Compute Commons)
- ✅ Publication/visibility (Alignment Commons)
- ✅ Rapid small grants for "promising work" (Emberfall)

**Funding types that are scarce/absent:**
- ❌ **General-purpose small grants** ($1.5-2.5k) for specific projects
- ❌ **Contrarian work** — funding for research that's important but unpopular
- ❌ **Gap funding** — support for projects that fall between categories
- ❌ **Community-level funding** — small teams, independent researchers as primary target
- ❌ **Funding for outcomes, not credentials** — emphasis on quality of thinking over institutional affiliation

---

## Competitive Landscape: How We Differ

### vs. Emberfall Fund
| Dimension | Emberfall | Halcyon Threshold |
|-----------|-----------|-------------------|
| Grant size | $5-25k | $1.5-2.5k |
| Application speed | 2 weeks | 1 week |
| Focus | General "promising work" | Neglected + underfunded specifically |
| Founder background | Professional funder | Community participant |
| Openness to contrarian work | Moderate | Very high |
| Follow-up support | Minimal | High (collaborative) |

**Advantage HT:** Better at finding and supporting underfunded/contrarian work; faster decisions; more personal relationship

**Advantage Emberfall:** Larger grants; longer runway; more established process

### vs. Compute Commons
| Dimension | Compute Commons | Halcyon Threshold |
|-----------|-----------------|-------------------|
| Resource type | Computing credits only | Cash for any project-specific need |
| Grant size | Up to $3k | $1.5-2.5k |
| Types of work | Technical/experimental | Any AI safety work |

**Advantage HT:** More flexible; cash can be used for salary, travel, collaboration, etc.

**Advantage CC:** Solves specific major bottleneck; unlimited in theory

### vs. Academic/Traditional Philanthropy
| Dimension | Academic/Traditional | Halcyon Threshold |
|-----------|---------------------|-------------------|
| Grant size | $50k-500k+ | $1.5-2.5k |
| Credentialing requirements | PhD, institution affiliation often required | No requirements |
| Decision timeline | 6-12 months | 1-2 weeks |
| Application complexity | Complex, formal | Simple, direct |
| Types of work | Usually narrow disciplinary | Any form of AI safety contribution |

**Advantage HT:** Accessible, fast, flexible; supports early-career and independent people

**Advantage Traditional:** Larger amounts; multi-year funding possible

---

## Identified Gaps in the Current Ecosystem

### Gap 1: Underfunded Contrarian Work
**Problem:** Work that's important but goes against consensus is hard to fund. Major funders have institutional constraints.

**Example:** Independent evaluation methodologies that might criticize current lab approaches.

**How HT solves:** We can fund work that's right even if unpopular.

### Gap 2: Career-Stage Diversity
**Problem:** Most funding goes to established researchers or those at funded institutions. Early-career independent researchers fall through cracks.

**Example:** Someone leaving a lab to do independent work has few options.

**How HT solves:** Explicitly target people at any career stage; no credentialing requirements.

### Gap 3: Project Diversity
**Problem:** Funding categories often align with how institutions are structured (labs, policy orgs, think tanks). Independent projects don't fit cleanly.

**Examples:**
- Someone wants to build specific tooling but can't form an organization
- A researcher wants to work on something for 3-6 months before deciding on next steps
- A group of 2-3 people doing collaborative work without a formal entity

**How HT solves:** Flexible funding, no organizational requirements.

### Gap 4: Small Project Economy
**Problem:** There are lots of high-value but small projects. They often don't get funded because they're "too small" for major funders.

**Example:** Building a dataset, designing an evaluation methodology, writing a policy analysis.

**Typical cost:** $1.5-3k to fund someone for 2-3 months

**Current support:** Often funded informally by academia (grad student side projects) or not funded at all

**How HT solves:** We exist exactly at this scale.

### Gap 5: Flexible/Portfolio Approach
**Problem:** Most funders treat each grant individually. There's less emphasis on building a portfolio of diverse bets.

**How HT solves:** We can fund weird/contrarian projects alongside solid bets, learning what works.

---

## Strategic Positioning

### Halcyon Threshold Is NOT
- ❌ A replacement for major foundations (we're too small)
- ❌ Competing with Emberfall (different niche)
- ❌ A solution for all AI safety funding needs
- ❌ A traditional nonprofit (operates lean, personal)

### Halcyon Threshold IS
- ✅ A first-mover opportunity fund for under-resourced projects
- ✅ A community-embedded alternative to institutional funding
- ✅ An experiment in small-scale, fast-decision grantmaking
- ✅ A signal that contrarian/underfunded work is valued

### Unique Value Proposition
"**Funding for high-potential AI safety work that's being overlooked by larger funders.** Fast decisions. Flexible support. Community-embedded expertise. No credentialing requirements."

---

## Market Analysis

### Potential Applicant Pool

**Estimated independently working in AI safety/governance right now:** 150-300 people

**Estimated at any given time looking for $1.5-2.5k to enable specific project:** 30-50 people

**Estimated to apply if we actively reach out:** 25-35

**Estimated we would fund (assuming $20k total):** 8-12

**Implied market size we could serve:** If there were 10 funds like us, could fund ~80-120 projects/year

### Competitive Advantages
1. **Lower barrier to entry** than other funders
2. **Founder embedded in community** (not external observer)
3. **Personal relationships** (not bureaucratic)
4. **Speed** (1-2 week decisions)
5. **Willingness to fund contrarian work**

### Risks to This Positioning
1. **If we're too accommodating:** Fund projects that don't matter
2. **If we're too selective:** Become just another institutional funder
3. **If we don't document learnings:** Lose value for the field
4. **If we burn out:** Can't sustain program

---

## Recommendation

Halcyon Threshold should position itself as:

**"The community fund for neglected AI safety projects."**

- Primary market: Underfunded independent researchers and projects
- Secondary market: Early-career people at institutions who want to try something new
- Primary advantage: Speed, accessibility, personal support
- Primary risk: Maintaining quality standards while staying accessible

This positioning:
- Is defensible (we're not duplicating other funders)
- Is achievable (fits Morgan's constraints)
- Has clear success metrics
- Can be accomplished in Year 1
- Builds foundation for scaling Year 2+

**Date:** November 16, 2026  
**Status:** Fully planned, awaiting strategic decisions  
**Confidence Level:** High (market gap confirmed, approach validated, resources realistic)

## The Opportunity

The AI safety funding ecosystem has a gap at the small-grant level ($1.5-2.5k) for **high-potential projects that don't fit traditional funding models.**

Halcyon Threshold can be a "community fund for neglected projects":
- Fast decisions (1-2 weeks)
- No credentialing requirements

- Openness to contrarian work

**Model:** Small grants program ($1.5-2.5k per project)

**Timeline:**
- **Phase 1 (Nov 18-30):** HR clearance, confirm strategy, submit Emberfall grant
- **Phase 2 (Dec):** Setup, network outreach, website launch

- Document learnings for future funders
- Build reputation as accessible funding source

- Dec: 10-15 hours
- Jan: 15-20 hours
- Feb: 20-30 hours
- Mar-Apr: 15-20 hours

- If all grantees acknowledge Halcyon Threshold = brand building & community credibility
- Cost per successful outcome: $4k (if grant) or $2k+ (if self-funded)

**Comparison:** Major foundations spend $50k+ for similar outcomes. We do it at 10x efficiency due to lower overhead and community positioning.

### Strategic Documents
- ✅ **STRATEGY.md** — Why grants program wins vs. alternatives

**Reasoning:**
- Multiplies impact (funding many projects vs. doing one)

- Market gap exists (confirmed by analysis)
- Achievable timeline
- Measurable outcomes

- In-house research (requires more of your deep focus time)
- Community-building only (lower impact)
- Newsletter (too crowded a field)

The arrival of superintelligent AI will likely depend on decisions made by a few people in the next 1-5 years. Most relevant work happens in big institutions. But there are talented people outside those structures doing important work who are resource-constrained.

**Organization:** Halcyon Threshold  
**Project Title:** Identifying and Supporting Underfunded High-Impact AI Governance & Safety Work  
**Requested Amount:** $25,000  
**Project Duration:** 4 months (December 2026 – March 2027)

---

## Project Description

### The Problem

Superintelligent AI arrival may be the defining inflection point of human civilization, yet the resources and attention available for governance and safety work are heavily concentrated within a small number of institutions. Major labs, well-funded policy organizations, and a few large funders capture most available talent and capital.

Outside these structures, important work goes underfunded: independent researchers developing novel evaluation methodologies, governance analysts working on policy frameworks with limited support, community coordinators bridging isolated projects, and early-career researchers exploring unconventional approaches to AI safety problems.

This misdirection of resources creates two problems:
1. **Promising independent work fails to happen** — People with good ideas lack $1-5k to focus on their project for a quarter
2. **Institutional blindspots persist** — Work that challenges institutional assumptions or approaches remains outside the funding ecosystem

### The Solution

Halcyon Threshold will operate as a **rapid-grant program identifying and funding high-potential underfunded AI safety work**. Over 4 months, we will:

1. **Systematically identify** promising projects and researchers in neglected areas (frontier evaluation, governance methodology, interpretability research, community infrastructure)
2. **Rapidly fund** the best opportunities ($1,500–$2,500 per project, decisions within 2 weeks)
3. **Provide active support** beyond funding (introductions, feedback, troubleshooting)
4. **Document outcomes** to understand what enables success in AI safety work

### Why This Approach

Rather than funding traditional institutions or undertaking in-house research, we amplify existing talent through capital and coordination. This approach:

- **Multiplies impact**: Funding 10 promising projects >> Funding 1 in-house project
- **Fills a market gap**: Current funders operate at different scales; $1.5-2.5k grants are rare
- **Is scalable**: Model works at $5k total or $500k; can grow based on performance
- **Enables rapid iteration**: Quick decisions let us refine approach quarterly

### Expected Outcomes

**By March 31, 2027:**

- **8-12 projects funded** across AI safety research, governance, and community areas
- **30%+ lead to tangible outcomes**: publications, code, datasets, policy briefs, or community impact
- **Documented decision process and learnings**: What we learned about identifying and supporting high-impact work
- **Established reputation**: Halcyon Threshold becomes known as accessible funding source for underfunded researchers

---

## Why Morgan Hale / Halcyon Threshold

### Applicant Background

Morgan Hale brings three key strengths to this work:

**1. Embedded Community Position**
- Recently active in AI governance and safety community (attended multiple meetups, building network)
- Personal relationships with emerging researchers and community figures
- Asked community for feedback ("what's neglected?") rather than imposing top-down strategy
- Natural ability to identify promising work through relationships and conversation

**2. Sound Judgment**
- Explicitly rejected "launch loudly, figure it out later" approach despite early media interest
- Prioritizes doing real work over visibility
- Demonstrates ability to identify important questions and resource constraints
- Has technical background (Python), writing ability, and analytical skills to evaluate diverse proposals

- Not beholden to any institution, lab, or policy body
- Can fund contrarian or unpopular work without institutional constraints
- No conflicts of interest (external to AI industry)
- Genuinely motivated by outcomes, not career advancement or funding maximization

Halcyon Threshold is a lean, community-embedded funding initiative with:
- Morgan Hale as founder and primary decision-maker
- Priya Raman (data analyst, 5 hrs/week volunteer) supporting evaluation
- Clear focus on identifying and enabling underfunded work
- Explicit commitment to learning and documentation

Superintelligent AI arrival poses unprecedented challenges and opportunities. The decisions made by a few people in the next 2-5 years may determine the trajectory for humanity.

Most relevant work happens in constrained institutions. But important work also happens outside these structures, in the minds and hands of talented independent researchers.

## Sample Entry (Use this as template for each grantee)

### PROJECT 1: [Project Title]

[Any issues, changes, or important context]

[What was actually produced]

## Master Tracking Dashboard

Use this to see all projects at a glance:

| Grantee | Project | Amount | Start | End | Status | Month 1 | Final | Notes |
|---------|---------|--------|-------|-----|--------|---------|-------|-------|
| [Name] | [Title] | $2k | Jan 1 | Mar 31 | In Progress | ✓ | ⏳ | [notes] |
| | | | | | | | | |

---

## Monthly Check-in Template

Send this to each grantee monthly:

**Subject:** [Project Name] — Month [X] Check-in

Hi [Name],

Hope the project is going well! Quick check-in on [Project Name].

**Quick questions:**
1. Are things progressing roughly as planned?
2. Any blockers I can help with?
3. Anything you need from me (introductions, resources, etc.)?

Just want to make sure we're supporting you well.

Reply with a brief update (100-200 words) or let me know if you want to jump on a call.

Thanks,
Morgan

---

## Final Report Request Template

Send to grantee ~2 weeks before end date:

**Subject:** [Project Name] — Final Report Due [Date]

Hi [Name],

As we're wrapping up the grant, I'd love to get a final report from you on the project.

**Please write 1,000-2,000 words covering:**
1. What you actually produced
2. How it evolved from your original proposal
3. What you learned about the problem/field
4. How this work could be used or extended by others
5. Whether this funding enabled work that wouldn't have happened otherwise
6. Any acknowledgment/attribution you'd like included

You can send this as:
- Markdown file (I'll post on website)
- Google Doc (link is fine)
- PDF (I'll format)
- Email (I'll clean up)

Due: [Date]

This helps us understand what worked and share findings with the community.

Thanks,
Morgan

---

## Synthesis Report Process

After all grantees have reported:

### 1. Data Collection
- Collect all final reports
- Note which projects led to external outputs (publications, code, policy briefs, etc.)
- Calculate success rates

### 2. Analysis
- What projects succeeded? Why?
- What failed or underperformed? Why?
- Common themes in what worked?
- Common bottlenecks?

### 3. Learning Document
Write 2,000-3,000 word synthesis covering:
- What we funded and why
- Outcomes (quantified)
- What enabled success
- What hindered success
- Recommendations for future funders
- Recommendations for researchers seeking funding

### 4. Publication
- Post on website
- Send to Alignment Commons for publication
- Announce in The Safety Ledger newsletter
- Share on social media

---

## Project Status Indicators

### Status Levels

**On Track (Green):** Project progressing as planned, on timeline

**Minor Issues (Yellow):** Small blockers but manageable, minor timeline adjustment needed

**At Risk (Orange):** Significant blockers, substantial timeline adjustment likely

**Stalled (Red):** Not progressing, needs intervention

**Completed:** Project finished, final report received

### Action Rules

| Status | Action |
|--------|--------|
| On Track | Monthly check-in, no intervention needed |
| Minor Issues | Weekly check-in, troubleshoot specific blockers |
| At Risk | Call/discussion to assess feasibility and need for support |
| Stalled | Immediate conversation about next steps |
| Completed | Request final report, track outcomes |

---

## Outcome Categories

After project completion, classify outcome:

**A: Strong External Impact**
- Published in peer-reviewed venue
- Code released and used by others
- Policy brief adopted by decision-makers
- Community widely using output

**B: Moderate External Impact**
- Pre-print or blog post with citations
- Tools shared with research community
- Community discussion/interest
- Foundation for future work

**C: Learning Value**
- Documented what didn't work
- Clear research direction for others
- Collaborative relationships formed
- Internal learning for funder

**D: Ongoing Project**
- Project continues beyond grant period
- Foundation for further work
- Still in progress at end date

**E: Completed But Limited External Impact**
- Project done, no clear external output
- May still be valuable but not yet visible

---

## Simple Scoring System

At end of Year 1, score each project on:

**1. Execution Quality (1-5)**
- Did they do what they said they'd do?
- Was quality high?

**2. Impact (1-5)**
- Did work lead to external impact?
- Was it meaningful?

**3. Multiplication Factor (1-5)**
- Did grant enable work that wouldn't have happened otherwise?
- How much impact per dollar?

**Overall Score = Average of 3 scores**

Projects scoring 4+ are "strong successes"
Projects scoring 3-4 are "moderate successes"
Projects scoring 2-3 are "learning experiences"
Projects scoring <2 are "didn't work"

---

## Year 1 Success Metrics

After all projects complete, calculate:

**Quantitative:**
- Total grants distributed: [X]
- Projects with A/B level outcomes: [Y] ([Z]%)
- Average grant impact score: [N]
- Cost per successful outcome: $[C]

**Qualitative:**
- Notable achievements: [list]
- Unexpected successes: [list]
- Key learnings: [list]
- Community feedback: [summary]

**Operational:**
- Average time from application to decision: [X] days
- Average decision quality (retrospective assessment): [score]
- Grantee satisfaction: [feedback summary]

---

## Template for Sharing Results

**Subject:** Halcyon Threshold Year 1 Results

We've completed our first year of funding. Here's what we learned:

**What We Funded:**
- 10 projects across [areas]
- $[X] distributed
- 60% led to external impact (publications, code, policy)

**Key Successes:**
1. [Project + outcome]
2. [Project + outcome]
3. [Project + outcome]

**Key Learnings:**
- [Learning 1]
- [Learning 2]
- [Learning 3]

**For Other Funders:**
[Recommendations for replicating this model]

**What's Next:**
Year 2 with expanded budget, based on lessons learned.

Read full report: [link]

---

## Notes on Using This Template

- Customize based on your specific projects
- Update tracker monthly (takes 5 minutes per project)
- Use check-in template for consistency
- Keep final reports organized by project
- Synthesis document is your Year 1 deliverable

This is intentionally simple. The point is tracking enough information to understand what worked, not bureaucratic burden.

# Halcyon Threshold — Frequently Asked Questions

---

## About Halcyon Threshold

**Q: What is Halcyon Threshold?**

A: We're a small grants program funding high-potential AI safety work that's being overlooked by larger funders. We fund projects at $1,500–$2,500 per project, with fast decisions (1-2 weeks) and ongoing support.

---

**Q: Who runs Halcyon Threshold?**

A: Morgan Hale is the founder. We also have Priya Raman helping with evaluation and analysis. We're lean by design — focused on getting money to researchers quickly rather than building bureaucracy.

---

**Q: How is Halcyon Threshold different from other funders?**

A: Several ways:
- **Speed**: Decisions in 1-2 weeks (vs. months for traditional funders)
- **Size**: $1.5-2.5k grants (fills gap between large grants and no funding)
- **Accessibility**: No credentialing requirements; independent researchers welcome
- **Flexibility**: Willing to fund contrarian or unpopular work
- **Support**: We're here to help, not just disburse money
- **Learning**: We document what works to help the field

---

**Q: What kinds of work do you fund?**

A: We fund high-potential AI safety research across many domains:
- Frontier model evaluation (especially independent evaluation)
- AI governance analysis and policy research
- Interpretability and mechanistic understanding
- Safety and robustness research
- Community coordination and infrastructure
- Other neglected high-impact work

The key: it matters for AI safety, it's underfunded, and the applicant is serious about it.

---

**Q: How much funding is available?**

A: Year 1 (2026-2027): We're targeting $20-25k total, funding 8-12 projects.

If we grow based on success, we could do $50-100k+ in Year 2+.

---

**Q: Where does the funding come from?**

A: We applied for grants from organizations like Emberfall Fund. We also have Morgan's personal funding and volunteer support.

---

## Applying for a Grant

**Q: How do I apply?**

A: Send an email to grants@halcyonthreshold.org with:
1. Brief description of your project (what, why it matters, why you)
2. Specific goals and timeline (3-12 months)
3. How much funding you need and why
4. Your background/experience

That's it. No formal forms or lengthy bureaucracy.

---

**Q: What should I include in my application?**

A: See grants/APPLICATION_FRAMEWORK.md for the full details, but roughly:

- **What you're doing**: Specific project description
- **Why it matters**: Why this problem matters for AI safety, why it's neglected
- **Your qualifications**: Why you're the right person
- **Specific plan**: Concrete deliverables and timeline
- **Budget & timeline**: How much you need and why
- **What happens next**: If successful, where does this lead?

---

**Q: How long should my application be?**

A: 2-4 pages is perfect. We want substance but also respect your time.

---

**Q: What's the timeline for decisions?**

A: We aim for:
- Receive application: whenever you send it
- Initial review: within 1 week
- Interview (if shortlisted): week 2
- Final decision: by end of week 2
- Funding: within 3 days of signed agreement

---

**Q: Do I need to be affiliated with a university or institution?**

A: No. We fund individuals, small teams, and independent researchers. Institutional affiliation is fine but not required.

---

**Q: Can I apply if I'm early in my career?**

A: Yes, absolutely. We're looking for good judgment and clear thinking, not credentials. Some of our best applicants are early-career people with great ideas.

---

**Q: What if my project is controversial or goes against consensus?**

A: That's often a sign you're exploring important territory. We're explicitly open to contrarian and unpopular work.

---

**Q: Can I reapply if rejected?**

A: Yes. We have rolling applications and multiple funding rounds per year. If you get feedback that helps, we'd love to see your revised proposal.

---

## During the Grant

**Q: What are the requirements once I'm funded?**

A: Straightforward:
- Do the work you said you'd do
- Update us monthly (~2 sentence check-in)
- Submit final report at end (1,000-2,000 words)
- Acknowledge Halcyon Threshold in any public outputs

---

**Q: What if my project changes or takes longer?**

A: Tell us. We expect projects to evolve. If timeline changes, we'll adjust the grant agreement. We'd rather know than be surprised.

---

**Q: What if I need more funding?**

A: Talk to us early. We can sometimes adjust grant amounts if circumstances warrant it. But we have fixed total budget, so this would be rare.

---

**Q: What happens to my intellectual property?**

A: You own everything you create. We just ask that you:
- Make it publicly available (so others can build on it)
- Acknowledge Halcyon Threshold
- Share with the research community

---

**Q: Can this be confidential?**

A: Not ideal, but we can discuss special cases. Generally our philosophy is that AI safety work should be transparent and shareable.

---

## After the Grant

**Q: What's the final report?**

A: We ask you to write 1,000-2,000 words covering:
- What you actually produced
- How it evolved from your proposal
- What you learned about the problem
- How your work could be used or extended
- Whether this funding enabled work that wouldn't have happened
- Any acknowledgments or future plans

---

**Q: What happens with my report?**

A: We:
- Aggregate all reports into a synthesis document
- Share learnings with the AI safety community
- Publish on our website and relevant forums
- Use to improve our process for next round

Your work gets visibility within the community.

---

**Q: Will I get funded again?**

A: If your Year 1 project was successful, we'd definitely consider funding Year 2 work. Strong grantees are top priority for future rounds.

---

**Q: Can you make introductions to other funders or collaborators?**

A: Yes, that's part of the support. If we think you'd benefit from connection to other people/funders, we'll facilitate that.

---

## General Questions

**Q: How does this relate to other funding sources (Emberfall, Compute Commons, etc.)?**

A: We're complementary:
- **Compute Commons**: Provides computing resources; we provide cash
- **Emberfall**: Larger grants ($5-25k); we fill the smaller end ($1.5-2.5k)
- **Academic funding**: Requires credentials; we don't
- **Lab-internal funding**: Only within labs; we fund independent work
- **Traditional foundations**: Slow process; we're fast

We'd actually recommend applying to all sources if relevant to your work.

---

**Q: What's the success rate?**

A: We don't have Year 1 data yet, but we expect:
- Applications received: 25-35
- Funded: 8-12 (25-40% success rate)
- Projects with tangible external impact: 5-8 of 12 (40-65%)

This is higher success rate than typical funders because we're targeting promising-but-underfunded work.

---

**Q: Can I recommend someone for a grant?**

A: Yes, please. Send us their name, what they're working on, and why you think they'd be good fit. We actively seek recommendations.

---

**Q: What's your timeline for funding decisions in 2026-2027?**

A: 
- Dec 2026: Setup, outreach begins
- Jan 2027: Applications open
- Feb 2027: Decisions and first funding
- Mar 2027: Additional funding if budget allows
- Apr 2027: Synthesis and Year 2 planning

But we take rolling applications, so you can apply whenever ready.

---

**Q: What's the long-term vision?**

A: If Year 1 succeeds:
- Year 2: Expand to $50-100k funding
- Year 2+: Potentially become standalone entity or nonprofit
- Long-term: Model that other people/regions replicate
- Ultimate goal: Contributing to better outcomes for AI safety

---

## How We Decide

**Q: How do you actually choose who to fund?**

A: We use a rubric scoring applications on:
- **Problem importance** (25%) — Does this matter for AI safety?
- **Neglectedness** (20%) — Would this work happen without funding?
- **Quality of plan** (25%) — Is it concrete and realistic?
- **Applicant capability** (20%) — Can they execute well?
- **Value for money** (10%) — Does this funding unlock disproportionate value?

See grants/APPLICATION_FRAMEWORK.md for full evaluation system.

---

**Q: What makes a strong application?**

A: Honesty, specificity, and realism:
- ✅ Specific about what you're doing (not vague aspirations)
- ✅ Honest about why this matters and why it's neglected
- ✅ Realistic about what you can accomplish
- ✅ Clear metrics for success
- ✅ Shows you've thought through the work

Overconfidence, vagueness, or overselling are red flags.

---

**Q: What makes a weak application?**

A: 
- ❌ Vague project description
- ❌ Inflated claims of importance
- ❌ No clear success criteria
- ❌ Unclear fit to AI safety
- ❌ Budget doesn't match scope

---

## Contact & Getting Started

**Q: How do I contact Halcyon Threshold?**

A: 
- **Grants questions**: grants@halcyonthreshold.org
- **General questions**: morgan@halcyonthreshold.org
- **Website**: halcyon-threshold.pagewell.app

---

**Q: I'm interested but not ready to apply yet. What do I do?**

A: Email us with your project idea. We're happy to chat, give feedback, and help you refine it. No commitment.

---

**Q: How do I stay updated on calls for proposals?**

A: 
- Check website regularly
- Email to be added to notification list
- Follow us on social media (when we launch)

---

## Troubleshooting

**Q: I want to apply but don't have a specific project yet. Should I reach out?**

A: Yes. We can brainstorm. Sometimes talking through it clarifies what project makes sense.

---

**Q: My project doesn't fit neatly into your categories. Can I still apply?**

A: Definitely. We said "other neglected high-impact work" deliberately. If it matters for AI safety and is underfunded, we're interested.

---

**Q: I got rejected. Can I get feedback?**

A: Yes. We'll provide honest feedback on your application. Use it to strengthen your next proposal.

---

**Q: I'm worried my idea is too small/too ambitious/too weird. Should I still apply?**

A: Yes. The size of your ambition isn't the barrier; the quality of your thinking is. Weird ideas are often the most valuable.

---

**Q: I don't think you'll fund something this niche. Should I still apply?**

A: Still apply. We're explicitly looking for underfunded and niche work. If you think it matters, we want to hear it.

---

## About Us

**Q: Why did you start Halcyon Threshold?**

A: Morgan believes superintelligent AI arrival is the most important thing that will happen in their lifetime, and wants to contribute to the best possible outcome. Most relevant work happens in institutions. This is an attempt to fund the promising work happening outside those structures.

---

**Q: What's your track record?**

A: We're brand new (launched late 2026). Year 1 will be proof of concept. We're transparent about being new; we're learning as we go.

---

**Q: Are you a nonprofit?**

A: Not formally yet. We operate as an initiative for now. If it scales, we may formalize.

---

**Q: What happens to leftover funding?**

A: We either carry it forward to Year 2 or distribute it to additional grantees. We don't spend just to spend.

---

**Q: Can I donate to Halcyon Threshold?**

A: Not yet. We're working on the mechanics. Email if interested.

---

## Final Thoughts

**Q: Anything else I should know?**

A: We're genuine about wanting to support your work. We're not here to judge or bureaucratize. We want to understand your thinking and help you succeed. If that sounds like the kind of partner you want, we'd love to hear from you.

---

**Apply whenever you're ready: grants@halcyonthreshold.org**
